elements.element: Customer may assign to an affiliate without consent.
elements.evidence: The rendered clause still requires the other party's express prior written consent for any assignment, and the new carve-out sentence covers only "a successor in a merger, acquisition, or sale of substantially all of its assets." No affiliate exception appears anywhere; to reach preferred the drafter must add an express Customer-to-affiliate transfer right without Vendor consent.

elements.element: Customer may assign to a successor in a merger, acquisition, or sale of substantially all assets without consent.
elements.evidence: "The foregoing consent requirement shall not apply to an assignment of this Agreement by either party to a successor in a merger, acquisition, or sale of substantially all of its assets, which may be made upon written notice to the other party." "Either party" includes Clear Capital (Company/Customer), and the only condition is written notice, not consent.

elements.element: Vendor may not assign without Customer's consent.
elements.evidence: The added carve-out is mutual ("by either party"), so RadialSpark may now assign to its own merger/acquisition successor on notice alone without Clear Capital's consent. For the preferred level the carve-out would have to be limited to Customer (e.g., "by the Company"), leaving Vendor assignments wholly consent-gated.

elements.element: Customer's consent to Vendor assignment is not to be unreasonably withheld.
elements.evidence: Retained Section 10 language: consent "will not be unreasonably withheld," applied mutually and therefore to Clear Capital's consent to a RadialSpark assignment.

elements.element: Vendor may never assign to a Customer competitor.
elements.evidence: No competitor bar appears in Section 10 as rendered; indeed the new mutual successor carve-out would permit RadialSpark to assign to an acquiring competitor of Clear Capital on notice. Preferred would require an express absolute prohibition on Vendor assignment to a Customer competitor.

elements.element: Customer's change of control gives Vendor no termination right.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: the Agreement contains no change-of-control termination or re-pricing right in favour of RadialSpark (rationale confirms none in Section 6, and none is created by the edit), so there is no such right to delete.

elements.element: Both parties may assign to a successor.
elements.evidence: "...an assignment of this Agreement by either party to a successor in a merger, acquisition, or sale of substantially all of its assets" — expressly mutual and expressly excepted from the consent requirement.

elements.element: A successor assignment requires written notice.
elements.evidence: "...which may be made upon written notice to the other party." Written notice is the sole condition on the successor carve-out.

Retained: "Neither party shall assign, transfer, or subcontract this Agreement or any of its obligations hereunder without the other party's express, prior written consent." The only carve-out added is the successor exception; no affiliate or other no-consent non-successor exception is retained or introduced.

elements.element: Consent to other assignments is not to be unreasonably withheld.
elements.evidence: Retained: "which will not be unreasonably withheld," and the edit leaves that qualifier untouched for all non-successor assignments, transfers and subcontracts.

reasons: The fallback checklist is complete on the operative text: a single added sentence supplies the mutual successor carve-out on written notice, while the original mutual consent requirement and the "not unreasonably withheld" standard survive verbatim to cover all other assignments.

The preferred level is not reached: there is no affiliate carve-out for Clear Capital, no competitor bar on RadialSpark, and the carve-out is mutual so RadialSpark can now assign to a successor without Clear Capital's consent. That is acceptable here only because the drafter expressly targeted the fallback, which itself mandates mutuality; the mutual exception is therefore not an intent failure.

Minimality holds: one inserted sentence, no deletions, no survival tail, no expense or procedural extras, and no duplication of the existing consent mechanic. The words "upon written notice to the other party" are required by the fallback element rather than surplus.

Intent is preserved: the subcontracting restriction, the consent standard and all cross-references remain intact, no defined term is left dangling, and no retained sentence contradicts the new carve-out (the carve-out is drafted as an express exception to "the foregoing consent requirement").

Classification as a deviation is supportable — before the edit the clause failed the fallback elements requiring a successor right on notice — though note this is not walk-away territory, since the original consent requirement was mutual and reasonableness-qualified rather than a blanket prohibition. The comment correctly states the fallback posture.
